sections.title: The hook
sections.intro_md:
Around the year 1500, the second-largest city on Earth, after Beijing, stood among the boulders of central Karnataka. Persian and Portuguese visitors wrote about its gem bazaars and war elephants. In 1565 it lost one battle and within months was looted, burned and abandoned. It was **Vijayanagara**, the city of victory. We call its ruins **Hampi**.

Today, 350 kilometres south, **Bengaluru** writes software for half the world's big companies.

Between those two cities sits a state of surprises: a dome where one clap returns fourteen echoes, a 57-foot statue cut from one rock in about 983, the iron rockets that taught Britain rocketry, a gold mine where physicists caught the first atmospheric neutrinos, and 71 per cent of India's coffee. Today you meet them one by one.

sections.title: Where you are
sections.intro_md:
Karnataka fills the south-western shoulder of the peninsula: a coast on the Arabian Sea, the wall of the Western Ghats behind it, and a high, dry plateau rolling east. Goa, Maharashtra, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu and Kerala border it.

The name is usually read as **karu nadu**, the elevated land. The state was formed on **1 November 1956** as Mysore State, from Kannada-speaking parts of five older units, and renamed **Karnataka** on 1 November 1973. Every 1 November is **Rajyotsava**, the state's birthday.

The numbers that carry it: sixth largest state, eighth most populous, two in three people speaking Kannada at home, 71 per cent of India's coffee, 45 per cent of its mulberry silk, and a per capita income close to double the national figure.

sections.title: The land
sections.intro_md:
Karnataka has three landscapes, and one day's drive crosses all of them. The **Karavali** coast has rice, palms and temple towns. The **Malnad**, the hill country of the Western Ghats, takes some of India's heaviest rain and grows coffee under shade trees. Over the crest lies the **Bayaluseeme**, the open Deccan plateau: dry, sunny, scattered with granite boulders and old tanks.

Most rivers rise in the Ghats and run east. The **Kaveri** feeds Mysuru, Bengaluru and, downstream, Tamil Nadu, which is why sharing it has been a legal fight for over a century. The **Krishna** and **Tungabhadra** water the north. Only short rivers like the Sharavathi run west, and the Sharavathi falls off the Ghats at Jog.

spotlights.name: Jog Falls
spotlights.spot_it: A ribbon of white water dropping 253 metres down a curved black cliff, in four separate streams.
spotlights.story_md: The Sharavathi river reaches the edge of the Western Ghats in Shivamogga district and simply falls off it. The drop at Jog is about **253 metres**, the third-highest waterfall in India by total height. It splits into four streams with names: **Raja**, a single unbroken column; **Rani**, a gentle sheet of foam; **Roarer**, which crashes into a basin; and **Rocket**, which shoots out in jets. The Linganamakki dam upstream takes much of the water for power, so come in August or September, when the gorge fills with mist.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Shows how the Western Ghats turn rain into power, scenery and conflict over water.
spotlights.memory_hook: Raja, Rani, Roarer, Rocket: the four Rs of Jog.

spotlights.name: Agumbe
spotlights.spot_it: A small village on a misty ridge, wet green forest falling away to the coast, with a sunset point over the Arabian Sea.
spotlights.story_md: Agumbe, at about 660 metres in Shivamogga district, is called the **Cherrapunji of the South**. Its mean annual rainfall is about 7,620 millimetres, most of it between June and September. The forest around it is one of the best places on Earth to find the **king cobra**, the world's longest venomous snake, and in 2005 the herpetologist Romulus Whitaker set up the Agumbe Rainforest Research Station to study it. Agumbe has a second fame: many episodes of the 1980s television series **Malgudi Days**, from R. K. Narayan's stories and directed by Shankar Nag, were filmed in its streets.
spotlights.why_it_matters: India's rainforest research and a national TV memory, in one village.
spotlights.memory_hook: Where it rains like Cherrapunji and Swami still walks the street.

spotlights.name: The Kaveri
spotlights.spot_it: A small tank in the hills of Kodagu, and far downstream a wide river spilling over rocks in a hundred falls.
spotlights.story_md: The Kaveri rises at **Talakaveri**, a spring and temple tank on Brahmagiri hill in Kodagu, and runs about 800 kilometres east to the Bay of Bengal. In Karnataka it fills the **Krishna Raja Sagara** reservoir, then splits round islands and pours off the plateau at **Shivanasamudra**. In 1902 a hydroelectric station at Shivanasamudra sent power along a 140-kilometre line to the Kolar Gold Fields, one of the earliest such schemes in Asia. The river's water has been argued over since agreements in 1892 and 1924; the Supreme Court set today's sharing formula in 2018, and every weak monsoon the fight returns.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The river that feeds Bengaluru and Tamil Nadu and keeps their politics tense.
spotlights.memory_hook: One river, two states, a hundred years of court dates.

sections.title: Elephants, tigers and a silver-maned monkey
sections.intro_md:
Karnataka's forests run in a continuous belt along the Western Ghats and down into the Nilgiri hills, where they join forests in Kerala and Tamil Nadu. That unbroken corridor is why the state holds about **a quarter of India's wild elephants** and about a tenth of its tigers, with **Bandipur** and **Nagarhole** among the best places in Asia to see both.

The state animal is the elephant, the state bird the **Indian roller**, and the state tree **sandalwood**, which once made the Mysore kingdom rich and later made the bandit Veerappan infamous.

Wildlife here lives close to people. Elephants raid crops, leopards walk through coffee estates, and the forest tribes of Nagarhole, such as the Jenu Kuruba, have spent decades fighting eviction from land they lived on before it became a park.

spotlights.name: Asian elephants of Bandipur and Nagarhole
spotlights.spot_it: Herds with calves gathering on the open shore of the Kabini reservoir in the dry season.
spotlights.story_md: In summer, when the forests dry out, elephants from Nagarhole, Bandipur and the neighbouring Kerala and Tamil Nadu forests walk down to the receding shores of the **Kabini reservoir**, which separates Nagarhole from Bandipur. Karnataka's forests hold about a quarter of India's wild elephants. India's first all-DNA count, released in 2025, put the national total at about **22,446**, lower than the 29,964 counted by older methods in 2017, a gap partly explained by the change in method.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The Nilgiri forests hold one of the largest elephant populations left in Asia.
spotlights.memory_hook: Every summer the elephants come to the beach at Kabini.

spotlights.name: Tigers of Bandipur and Nagarhole
spotlights.spot_it: A tiger crossing a dusty forest track among teak and bamboo, often seen from a jeep.
spotlights.story_md: **Bandipur** became one of India's first tiger reserves under Project Tiger in **1973**. Nagarhole, next door, became a tiger reserve in 2003. Together with Mudumalai and Wayanad across the border, they form one of the densest tiger landscapes anywhere. India held an estimated **3,682** wild tigers in 2022, about three-quarters of the world's total, and Karnataka is one of the top two or three states. Nagarhole is also where long-term camera-trap studies helped pioneer the scientific counting of tigers in India.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Karnataka is a stronghold of the world's largest wild tiger population.
spotlights.memory_hook: Project Tiger's first class of 1973 included Bandipur.

sections.title: Ashoka to the Chalukyas
sections.intro_md:
Karnataka's written history starts with an emperor from the north. **Ashoka's** edicts, carved in the 3rd century BCE, have been found at several places in the state, and one of them, at **Maski**, was the first ever found to name him directly.

The first kingdom of Kannada speakers was the **Kadamba** dynasty of Banavasi, from the 4th century CE. A Kadamba-era stone at Halmidi is the oldest known Kannada inscription. Then came the **Chalukyas of Badami** (about 540 to 753), who carved cave temples into red cliffs and experimented with every way of building a temple. Their greatest king, **Pulakeshin II**, stopped the northern emperor Harsha at the Narmada.

After them the **Rashtrakutas** (753 to 982) ruled much of India from Manyakheta. Their king Amoghavarsha I is linked to the **Kavirajamarga** of about 850, the oldest surviving book in Kannada.

spotlights.name: Maski, where Ashoka got his name
spotlights.spot_it: A small town in the dry plains of Raichur below a rocky hill with an old edict on a boulder.
spotlights.story_md: For a century after James Prinsep deciphered the Brahmi script in 1837, historians read edicts by a king who called himself only **Devanampiya Piyadasi**, 'beloved of the gods, of gracious look'. Linking him to the Ashoka of Buddhist chronicles was a guess. In **1915** a gold-mining engineer, C. Beadon, found a minor rock edict at **Maski** in Raichur district. It begins with 'Devanampiyasa Asokasa', naming Ashoka outright for the first time and settling the question. Maski was also a gold-working site in ancient times.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A boulder in Karnataka confirmed the identity of India's most famous emperor.
spotlights.memory_hook: The rock that told us Piyadasi was Ashoka.

spotlights.name: The Halmidi inscription
spotlights.spot_it: A short stone pillar with 16 lines of rounded early letters, now standing as a replica in a village near Belur.
spotlights.story_md: In **1936**, M. H. Krishna, the Mysore state's director of archaeology, read a stone at **Halmidi** in Hassan district. Its 16 lines, a royal grant from the Kadamba period, are written in Kannada in the Kadamba script, making it the **oldest known Kannada inscription**. It is usually dated to about 450 to 500 CE, though some scholars argue for the later 6th century. The original is kept in Mysuru; Halmidi has a fibreglass copy. The stone was central to the case that won Kannada **classical language** status from the Government of India in 2008.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The birth certificate of written Kannada.
spotlights.memory_hook: Kannada's first written words are a land grant.

spotlights.name: Badami cave temples
spotlights.spot_it: Four cave shrines cut into a red sandstone cliff above a green tank, with giant gods carved on their walls.
spotlights.story_md: The early Chalukyas made **Badami** (ancient Vatapi) their capital in the 6th century and cut four cave temples into the cliff above the Agastya tank: three Hindu, for Shiva and Vishnu, and one Jain. Cave 3, dedicated to Vishnu, carries an inscription of 578 CE and a 2.5-metre-tall Vishnu seated on the serpent, plus Varaha lifting the earth and Narasimha. Cave 1 has an 18-armed dancing Shiva. The caves are cut, not built: every pillar and ceiling is the living rock.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The start of the great south Indian temple tradition.
spotlights.memory_hook: A palace for the gods carved, not built, out of a cliff.

spotlights.name: Pattadakal
spotlights.spot_it: Ten stone temples on a riverbank lawn, some with northern beehive towers and some with southern stepped towers, side by side.
spotlights.story_md: **Pattadakal**, on the Malaprabha river, was where the Chalukya kings were crowned. Its ten main temples, nine Hindu and one Jain, were built in the 7th and 8th centuries and mix the northern **Nagara** and southern **Dravida** styles in one place, which is why UNESCO listed it in **1987**. The largest, the **Virupaksha temple**, was built about 740 by Queen **Lokamahadevi** to celebrate her husband's victory over the Pallavas of Kanchipuram. Its walls carry scenes from the Ramayana, the Mahabharata and the Panchatantra. The Pallavas had sacked Badami a century earlier; this was the reply in stone.
spotlights.why_it_matters: North and south India's two temple languages meet on one lawn.
spotlights.memory_hook: A queen's victory temple, built to answer a sack.

sections.title: Soapstone lace and a giant in granite
sections.intro_md:
Between about 950 and 1346 the **Hoysalas** ruled southern Karnataka from Belur and then Halebidu. Their legend begins with a young man named Sala who killed a tiger to save his teacher; 'Hoy, Sala!' ('Strike, Sala!') is said to have given the dynasty its name, and the scene became its emblem.

Hoysala builders worked in **chloritic schist**, a soapstone soft enough to carve like wood when fresh and hard when it weathers. Their temples sit on star-shaped platforms and are covered from plinth to roof in friezes so fine that jewellery on a dancer's ankle can be counted. Many sculptors signed their work. In **2023** UNESCO listed three of them, at Belur, Halebidu and **Somanathapura**, together as the **Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas**.

Long before, the Ganga dynasty had given Karnataka its largest single sculpture: the Jain saint Bahubali at Shravanabelagola.

spotlights.name: Chennakeshava Temple, Belur
spotlights.spot_it: A low, star-shaped temple on a platform, every surface covered in carving, with dancers hanging from the eaves like brackets.
spotlights.story_md: King **Vishnuvardhana** consecrated the Chennakeshava temple at Belur in **1117**, reportedly to mark a victory over the Cholas. It took over a century to finish in its present form. The most loved carvings are the **madanikas**, celestial dancers on the brackets under the roof: one looks into a mirror, one is plucking a thorn, one is followed by a monkey tugging at her sari. Vishnuvardhana had been a Jain and became a Vaishnava under the philosopher **Ramanuja**, while his queen **Shantala Devi**, a celebrated dancer, stayed Jain.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Peak Hoysala craft in a temple still in daily worship.
spotlights.memory_hook: A queen who danced, a king who converted, a temple full of dancers.

spotlights.name: Hoysaleswara Temple, Halebidu
spotlights.spot_it: A long twin temple whose outer walls are wrapped in stacked bands of carving: elephants at the bottom, then lions, horsemen, scrolls and epic scenes.
spotlights.story_md: Halebidu, 'old capital', was **Dwarasamudra**, the Hoysala capital from the 1060s. Its twin-shrined Hoysaleswara temple has outer walls carved in horizontal bands: a long procession of elephants at the base, no two alike, then lions, horsemen, scrolling vines and scenes from the Ramayana, Mahabharata and Bhagavata Purana, with gods larger than life above. In **1311** the Delhi general **Malik Kafur** sacked the city, and it was raided again in 1327. The temple's towers were never finished, which is why it looks flat-topped.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The densest storytelling in stone in south India.
spotlights.memory_hook: A wall where every elephant has its own face.

spotlights.name: Gommateshwara, Shravanabelagola
spotlights.spot_it: A 17-metre nude figure of a man standing straight, arms at his sides, with creepers carved winding up his legs, on top of a granite hill.
spotlights.story_md: In about **983**, **Chavundaraya**, a minister of the Western Ganga dynasty, had a granite hilltop at Shravanabelagola carved into a statue of **Bahubali**, the Jain prince who renounced his kingdom. It is about **57 feet (17 metres)** tall and cut from a single block, one of the largest free-standing monoliths in the world. Bahubali stood in meditation so long that vines grew up his legs and anthills formed at his feet, and the sculptors carved both. Every 12 years the **Mahamastakabhisheka** bathes him from scaffolding in milk, saffron, sandal paste and flowers. The last was in 2018; the next is due in **2030**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Karnataka was a great centre of Jainism for over a thousand years.
spotlights.memory_hook: Stand still long enough and the vines climb you.

sections.title: The city of victory and the sultans
sections.intro_md:
In **1336**, two brothers, Harihara and Bukka, founded a kingdom on the Tungabhadra that grew into the **Vijayanagara empire**, ruling most of south India for two centuries. Its capital at Hampi had walls in seven rings, bazaars for horses and gems, and water channels that still run. Scholars estimate it was the second-largest city in the world around 1500, after Beijing.

Its rivals were the Deccan sultanates that grew out of the **Bahmani** kingdom, based first at Gulbarga and then Bidar. In **1565**, at the battle of Talikota, an alliance of sultans defeated Vijayanagara. The city was looted and burned for months and never recovered.

The sultans built too. Bijapur's Adil Shahi rulers raised domes and mosques, and Bidar's metalworkers invented a black-and-silver craft. North Karnataka is still marked by both traditions.

spotlights.name: Hampi
spotlights.spot_it: A tall whitewashed temple tower above a river, surrounded by kilometres of ruined halls, gateways and bazaars among orange boulders.
spotlights.story_md: **Hampi** was the heart of Vijayanagara from 1336 to 1565. Its ruins cover about 4,187 hectares and include more than 1,600 surviving structures: temples, palaces, stepped tanks, elephant stables and a 'Lotus Mahal' with Islamic arches. The **Virupaksha temple** is the one place that never stopped worship; its gopuram still rises over the bazaar street. The Persian envoy Abdur Razzaq, who visited in the 1440s, said the eye had never seen a place like it. UNESCO listed Hampi in **1986** and put it on the danger list from 1999 to 2006 because of new bridges and roads.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The ruins of one of the largest cities of the medieval world.
spotlights.memory_hook: In 1500 only Beijing was bigger.

spotlights.name: The stone chariot of Hampi
spotlights.spot_it: A small stone shrine shaped like a temple chariot, with carved stone wheels, in front of a pillared hall: the image on India's ₹50 note.
spotlights.story_md: In the courtyard of the **Vittala temple** stands a shrine to Garuda, Vishnu's eagle, built in the shape of a processional chariot. Its wheels once turned on their axles, guides say, before they were fixed with cement to protect them. It is the single most recognisable image of Karnataka and since August 2017 has appeared on the back of India's **₹50** note. The Vittala temple's mandapa nearby has slender granite pillars that ring with musical notes when tapped, which is why visitors are no longer allowed to touch them.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Karnataka's most famous image, now in every Indian's wallet.
spotlights.memory_hook: A chariot that will never move, on a note that never stops moving.

spotlights.name: Gol Gumbaz
spotlights.spot_it: A huge plain cube with a grey dome and seven-storey towers at each corner, rising out of Vijayapura.
spotlights.story_md: **Gol Gumbaz** is the tomb of **Mohammed Adil Shah**, the seventh sultan of Bijapur, who died in **1656**; work stopped then and it was left unfinished. The dome is about 44 metres across on the outside, among the largest of its age anywhere, and the building is 60.5 metres high. Inside, a gallery runs round the base of the dome. Whisper against the wall and someone on the far side hears you clearly. Clap once and the sound comes back again and again: in experiments in 1945, a single clap produced as many as **14 distinct echoes**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The largest dome in India, and an acoustic toy on a royal scale.
spotlights.memory_hook: Clap once, hear it fourteen times.

sections.title: Mysore, Tipu and the women who fought
sections.intro_md:
After Vijayanagara fell, its southern governors, the **Wadiyars** of Mysore, took over the old capital's rituals, including Dasara. In the 18th century two soldiers, **Hyder Ali** and his son **Tipu Sultan**, took real power and fought the East India Company in four wars. Tipu died defending Srirangapatna in **1799**. The British restored the Wadiyars, and under Krishnaraja Wadiyar IV and his Diwan, the engineer **M. Visvesvaraya**, who built the KRS dam on the Kaveri, Mysore became one of India's best-run princely states.

Resistance came from small places too. **Kittur**, a little kingdom near Belagavi, fought the Company in 1824 under a queen. **Chitradurga** remembers a woman with a rice pestle.

In 1956 the Kannada-speaking districts of Bombay, Hyderabad, Madras, Coorg and Mysore were joined into one state, after a campaign that had begun at the start of the century.

spotlights.name: Tipu Sultan
spotlights.spot_it: A bearded ruler in a turban and green robes, with tiger stripes on his throne, his flags and his soldiers' coats.
spotlights.story_md: **Tipu Sultan** was born in **1751** at Devanahalli, near today's Bengaluru airport, and ruled Mysore from **1782** until he died fighting at the breach of Srirangapatna on **4 May 1799**. He reformed coinage and the calendar, encouraged silk and Channapatna toys, built a navy and wrote to France and the Ottomans for allies against the British. He used the tiger as his emblem. His legacy is fought over in Karnataka today: some call him a freedom fighter, others point to forced conversions in Kodagu and Malabar. Historians disagree on how much of the darker record came from British propaganda.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The ruler the British feared most in south India, and still a political argument.
spotlights.memory_hook: The Tiger of Mysore died at the breach.

spotlights.name: The Mysorean rockets
spotlights.spot_it: Iron tubes about the length of a forearm, lashed to long bamboo or sword-blade poles, fired in volleys.
spotlights.story_md: Hyder Ali and Tipu Sultan's armies fired the first successful **iron-cased rockets**. An iron tube held more powder at higher pressure than the paper and wood casings used in Europe, so the rockets flew up to about **2 kilometres**. At **Pollilur** in 1780 a rocket reportedly blew up a British ammunition store. After 1799 the British shipped captured rockets to the Woolwich Arsenal, and **William Congreve** developed his own rockets from them, used against Napoleon and the United States. Since 2002, more than 3,000 have been dug up from a well at Nagara in Shivamogga district.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Modern military rocketry began in Karnataka.
spotlights.memory_hook: Britain learned rocketry by losing to Mysore.

spotlights.name: Tipu's Tiger
spotlights.spot_it: A life-size painted wooden tiger savaging a man in a European coat; turn a handle and it growls while the man wails.
spotlights.story_md: This automaton was made for Tipu in the 1790s. Inside the tiger's body is a small pipe organ: turn the crank and bellows make the tiger snarl and the victim, in a red coat, groan, while his arm flaps. It sums up Tipu's view of the East India Company. After Srirangapatna fell in 1799, the British looted it and shipped it to London, where it was displayed in the East India Company's museum, delighting visitors including the poet John Keats. It is now one of the most popular objects in the **Victoria and Albert Museum**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A toy that is also a manifesto, now in a London museum.
spotlights.memory_hook: A tiger that eats a redcoat on demand.

spotlights.name: Rani Chennamma of Kittur
spotlights.spot_it: A queen on horseback with a raised sword, in statues across north Karnataka.
spotlights.story_md: **Chennamma** (1778 to 1829) was regent of **Kittur**, a small state near Belagavi. After her husband and son died she adopted an heir, Shivalingappa. The East India Company refused to recognise him, an early version of the 'doctrine of lapse' later used to annex whole kingdoms. In **October 1824** Kittur's forces beat back the Company, and the Dharwad collector **St John Thackeray** was killed. A second, bigger force captured her; she died a prisoner at Bailhongal in 1829. Her lieutenant **Sangolli Rayanna** fought on as a guerrilla until he was betrayed and hanged. Kittur celebrates her victory every October.
spotlights.why_it_matters: She fought the Company 33 years before 1857.
spotlights.memory_hook: A queen who won first and lost later.

sections.title: Kannada and the other tongues
sections.intro_md:
Kannada is a **Dravidian** language with about 44 million native speakers and some 15 million more who speak it as a second language. Its rounded script grew out of the 5th-century Kadamba script, and it became a **classical language** of India in 2008. Its oldest surviving book, the **Kavirajamarga** of about 850, is a guide to writing poetry.

Only two in three residents speak Kannada at home. Urdu, Telugu, Tamil, Marathi, **Tulu**, Lambadi, **Konkani** and **Kodava** fill the rest. Language is political here: signboard rules, school medium and jobs for Kannadigas are recurring fights, and the red-and-yellow Kannada flag flies everywhere on 1 November.

spotlights.name: Eight Jnanpiths
spotlights.spot_it: Eight writers, one shelf: Kuvempu, Bendre, Karanth, Masti, Gokak, Ananthamurthy, Karnad, Kambara.
spotlights.story_md: The Jnanpith is India's highest literary award. Kannada writers have won it **eight** times: **Kuvempu** (1967), **D. R. Bendre** (1973), **K. Shivaram Karanth** (1977), **Masti Venkatesha Iyengar** (1983), **V. K. Gokak** (1990), **U. R. Ananthamurthy** (1994), **Girish Karnad** (1998) and **Chandrashekhara Kambara** (2010). Only Hindi, with 12, has more. The list covers poets, a novelist who also wrote an encyclopaedia for children, the writer of the caste novel **Samskara**, and a playwright who also acted in Bollywood films. A language spoken by about one in twenty Indians has produced one in seven Jnanpiths.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A small language with a giant literary record.
spotlights.memory_hook: One in twenty Indians, one in seven Jnanpiths.

spotlights.name: Kuvempu
spotlights.spot_it: A poet in thick-rimmed spectacles, whose words open every school day in Karnataka.
spotlights.story_md: **Kuppali Venkatappa Puttappa** (1904 to 1994), who wrote as Kuvempu, grew up in the Malnad village of Kuppali. He became the first Kannada writer to win the Jnanpith, in 1967, for **Sri Ramayana Darshanam**, a modern epic retelling of the Ramayana. As vice-chancellor of Mysore University he pushed for teaching in Kannada. He wrote the state anthem, **'Jaya Bharata Jananiya Tanujate'**, and preached a philosophy of **Vishwa Manava**, the universal human, beyond caste and creed. Shivamogga airport and a train, the Vishwamanava Express, carry his name.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The voice of modern Kannada, sung at every school assembly.
spotlights.memory_hook: A poet who asked people to be universal humans.

spotlights.name: Banu Mushtaq and Heart Lamp
spotlights.spot_it: A writer in a headscarf holding a book with a lamp on its cover, the first Kannada book to win the International Booker.
spotlights.story_md: **Banu Mushtaq**, born in Hassan in 1948, is a lawyer, activist and short-story writer who started writing at 29 while struggling with postpartum depression. Her stories, mostly about Muslim women in small-town Karnataka, were translated by **Deepa Bhasthi** as **Heart Lamp**. On **20 May 2025** it won the International Booker Prize: the first Kannada book to win, the first short-story collection, and Bhasthi the first Indian translator to win. In September 2025 the state invited her to open the Mysuru Dasara; the BJP objected, courts dismissed the petitions, and she opened it.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Kannada's arrival on the world's biggest translated-fiction stage.
spotlights.memory_hook: A lamp lit in Hassan, seen in London.

sections.title: Faith and philosophy
sections.intro_md:
In 2011, 84 per cent of the state was Hindu, 12.9 per cent Muslim, 1.9 per cent Christian and 0.7 per cent Jain. Those numbers hide how much religious thinking began here.

Three of the great teachers of Hindu philosophy are tied to Karnataka. **Adi Shankara** founded his first matha at **Sringeri**. **Ramanuja** spent years in exile at Melkote. **Madhvacharya** was born near Udupi and founded the Krishna Matha there. In the 12th century **Basava** led a movement that rejected caste and temple ritual and gave rise to the **Lingayats**, today one of the state's largest and most politically important communities.

Jains built Shravanabelagola. Sufis built the dargah of Khwaja Bande Nawaz in Kalaburagi. Tibetan refugees built India's largest Nyingma monastery at Bylakuppe. And on the coast, people still bring their disputes to spirits in all-night rituals.

spotlights.name: Basava and the vachanas
spotlights.spot_it: A saint-statesman with a small linga hung on a cord at his chest; giant statues of him sit at Basavakalyan and in front of the Parliament.
spotlights.story_md: **Basava** (1131 to 1196) was a minister in the court of the Kalachuri king Bijjala II at Kalyana, now Basavakalyan in Bidar district. He said the body itself is a temple, rejected caste, gender discrimination and ritual sacrifice, and gave every follower, whatever their birth, an **ishtalinga**, a small personal linga worn on the body. He set up the **Anubhava Mantapa**, a hall where men and women of any caste debated spiritual questions. He and his followers wrote **vachanas**, short, plain Kannada prose poems. 'The rich will make temples for Shiva. What shall I, a poor man, do? My legs are pillars, the body the shrine.'
spotlights.why_it_matters: A 12th-century social revolution that still shapes Karnataka's politics.
spotlights.memory_hook: My legs are pillars, the body the shrine.

spotlights.name: Sri Krishna Matha, Udupi
spotlights.spot_it: A temple where devotees see Krishna not through a door but through a small silver window with nine holes.
spotlights.story_md: **Madhvacharya** founded the Krishna temple at Udupi in the 13th century. Worshippers see the image through a nine-holed window, the Navagraha Kindi. Nearby is the **Kanakana Kindi**: the story goes that the poet-saint **Kanakadasa**, barred from entering because he was not a Brahmin, sang outside, the wall cracked, and Krishna turned to face him. Eight mathas run the temple in turn, each for two years, a rotation called **Paryaya**. The temple feeds thousands of pilgrims every day, which earned it the name 'Anna Brahma', and gave the world Udupi cuisine.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A temple whose kitchen became India's most exported restaurant style.
spotlights.memory_hook: God turned around for the shepherd poet.

spotlights.name: Bhuta Kola

where.label: Tulu Nadu, Dakshina Kannada and Udupi

spotlights.spot_it: A night ritual: a performer in a towering halo of areca palm fronds, face painted yellow, dancing to drums and speaking as a spirit.
spotlights.story_md: On the Tulu coast, villages worship **bhutas** or **daivas**, local spirits such as **Panjurli**, the boar spirit that protects crops, and **Guliga**, the most widely worshipped. In a **kola**, a performer from a hereditary community, often Pambada, Parava or Nalike, is dressed and painted for hours, drinks toddy, and at the climax becomes the spirit. Villagers bring disputes, and the spirit's word settles them, so the ritual works as a village court. After the films **Kantara** (2022) and **Kantara: Chapter 1** (2025) made it famous, the state began a monthly allowance for performers over 60.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Living folk religion that doubles as justice.
spotlights.memory_hook: On kola night, the spirit is the judge.

sections.title: Drums, crowns and the music of two traditions
sections.intro_md:
Karnataka is the only state where both of India's classical music systems are at home. The south, around Mysuru, belongs to **Carnatic** music, whose method of teaching was organised by Purandara Dasa in Vijayanagara. The north, around **Dharwad** and Hubballi, produced an astonishing run of **Hindustani** singers: Bhimsen Joshi, Gangubai Hangal, Mallikarjun Mansur, Basavaraj Rajguru and Kumar Gandharva, who was born in Belagavi district.

The coast has **Yakshagana**, an all-night dance-drama with giant crowns, and the tiger dancers of Udupi. The plains have **Dollu Kunitha**, the drum dance of the Kuruba shepherds.

And then there is Kannada cinema, Sandalwood, which for decades revolved around one actor, **Rajkumar**, and in 2025 produced the year's highest-grossing Indian film, Kantara: Chapter 1.

Huge crowns, painted faces, layered skirts

spotlights.name: Yakshagana
spotlights.spot_it: Actors in towering gilded crowns and vivid face paint, whirling to loud chande drums, while a singer at the side tells the story.
spotlights.story_md: **Yakshagana** is the coast's great theatre. A troupe stages an episode from the Ramayana, Mahabharata or Puranas from dusk to dawn in a temple yard or a tent. The **bhagavata**, the lead singer, sings the story and directs the show; the actors dance, then speak improvised dialogue. Two drums drive it: the loud **chande** and the softer **maddale**. There are two main styles: **Tenkutittu** to the south around Mangaluru and **Badagutittu** to the north around Udupi. The earliest written mention is a 1556 inscription; the poet Parthi Subba wrote for it around 1600. Men played all the roles until recently; women now perform too.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The living theatre of the coast, older than most of India's modern stages.
spotlights.memory_hook: A crown, a drum and a whole night.

spotlights.name: Dollu Kunitha
spotlights.spot_it: A row of men with big barrel drums hung from their shoulders, beating and leaping in unison as a leader with cymbals calls the rhythm.
spotlights.story_md: **Dollu Kunitha** is the drum dance of the **Kuruba**, the shepherd community of the plains. The dollu drum is kept in temples of the deity **Beereshwara** and beaten during worship. A troupe of about a dozen men stands in a semicircle around a leader with cymbals, beating the heavy drums while jumping, turning and forming patterns. It is loud, fast and physical, and it is the standard opener of state parades and Rajyotsava. Women's troupes, rare a generation ago, now perform it too.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Karnataka's sound at every public celebration.
spotlights.memory_hook: Beat the drum, jump with it.

spotlights.name: Huli Vesha, the tiger dance
spotlights.spot_it: Men painted head to toe in yellow and black stripes, prowling and somersaulting through the streets of Udupi and Mangaluru to drums.
spotlights.story_md: During Navaratri, troupes of young men in coastal Karnataka paint themselves as **tigers**, the animal favoured by the goddess Durga. A troupe of five to ten has three to five 'tigers' and a band of **thaase** drummers. They roam the streets, stop at homes and shops for ten-minute shows, and collect money. Performers do handstands, somersaults and fire-breathing. The paint burns the skin and stays on for days, which is part of the vow. The dance began at Krishna Janmashtami and Ganesha festivals in Udupi before becoming a Dasara staple.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Folk devotion that is also street acrobatics and fundraising.
spotlights.memory_hook: For nine nights, Udupi has more tigers than Bandipur.

spotlights.name: Purandara Dasa
spotlights.spot_it: Every Carnatic music student's first lesson, sa-ri-ga-ma in raga Mayamalavagowla, goes back to him.
spotlights.story_md: **Purandara Dasa** (about 1470 to 1564) was born Srinivasa Nayaka, a rich merchant, who gave away his wealth to become a wandering devotee of Vishnu. He composed thousands of songs in simple Kannada. His lasting gift was a **teaching system**: graded exercises, the swaravalis and alankaras, all in the scale **Mayamalavagowla**, which is still how Carnatic music is taught everywhere. That is why he is called the **Pitamaha**, the grandfather, of Carnatic music. A hall named for him stands beside the Vittala temple at Hampi.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The man who designed the curriculum of south Indian classical music.
spotlights.memory_hook: Grandfather of Carnatic music, and a merchant who gave it all away.

spotlights.name: Dharwad's Hindustani singers
spotlights.spot_it: Old recordings of big, open voices from a small north Karnataka district: Bhimsen Joshi, Gangubai Hangal, Mallikarjun Mansur.
spotlights.story_md: **Bhimsen Joshi** (1922 to 2011), born in the old Dharwad district, ran away from home at 11 to find a music teacher, travelling as far as Gwalior. He trained with **Sawai Gandharva** of the **Kirana gharana**, and became the best-known Hindustani singer of his age, opening the 1988 song **Mile Sur Mera Tumhara**. He received the Bharat Ratna. **Gangubai Hangal** (1913 to 2009), from the same district and gharana, sang with a deep, powerful voice for seven decades. Few places of Dharwad's size have produced so many front-rank classical singers.
spotlights.why_it_matters: North Karnataka is a capital of Hindustani music.
spotlights.memory_hook: A boy ran away at 11 and came back a Bharat Ratna.

spotlights.name: Rajkumar and Sandalwood
spotlights.spot_it: A beloved film star whose face hangs in shops, rickshaws and offices across the state; and his son Puneeth.
spotlights.story_md: **Rajkumar** (1929 to 2006) acted in about **205** Kannada films and sang about 300 songs, winning a national award for playback singing. He received the Dadasaheb Phalke Award in 1995. In the 1980s he led the **Gokak agitation**, which demanded Kannada as the first language in schools. In **2000** the forest brigand **Veerappan** kidnapped him from his farmhouse in Gajanur and held him for **108 days**. He donated his eyes at death. His youngest son **Puneeth Rajkumar**, also a star, died suddenly in 2021; the outpouring of grief inspired a wave of eye donations.
spotlights.why_it_matters: One actor became a symbol of Kannada pride.
spotlights.memory_hook: 108 days in the jungle with Veerappan.

sections.title: Silk, sandalwood, toys and black metal
sections.intro_md:
Many of Karnataka's crafts were built by kings. Tipu Sultan brought in silkworms and encouraged toy makers. The Wadiyars set up a silk factory in 1912 and a soap factory in 1916. The Bahmani sultans brought Persian metalworkers to Bidar.

Several of these crafts carry **Geographical Indication** tags, India's legal protection for products tied to a place: Mysore silk, Channapatna toys, Bidriware, Ilkal sarees, Mysore Sandal Soap, Mysore painting and Kasuti embroidery among them.

Learn to recognise five things today: a plain silk saree with a pure gold border (Mysore), a brightly lacquered wooden top (Channapatna), a black vase with silver flowers (Bidar), a red-bordered cotton saree with a white-patterned pallu (Ilkal), and a gold-raised painting of a goddess (Mysore).

spotlights.name: Mysore silk
spotlights.spot_it: A plain, glossy single-colour silk saree with a narrow border of real gold zari and no busy pattern.
spotlights.story_md: Karnataka produces about **9,000 tonnes** of mulberry silk a year, nearly **45 per cent** of India's total. Silkworms are reared around **Ramanagara**, whose cocoon market is one of the largest in Asia; the thread is reeled at T. Narasipura and woven at the state-owned **KSIC** factory in Mysuru, founded by the Maharaja in **1912**. A Mysore silk saree is famous for its simplicity and for its zari, which the corporation says is made with 65 per cent silver and 0.65 per cent gold. Each saree now carries a hologram to beat fakes.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Silk is a rural livelihood for lakhs of families in southern Karnataka.
spotlights.memory_hook: Plain silk, real gold, and a hologram to prove it.

spotlights.name: Channapatna toys
spotlights.spot_it: Smooth, rounded wooden toys in shiny red, yellow, green and blue lacquer: tops, rattles, stacking rings and dolls.
spotlights.story_md: **Channapatna**, between Bengaluru and Mysuru, is called **Gombegala Ooru**, toy town. Its craftsmen turn soft **ivory-wood** (Wrightia tinctoria) on lathes and colour it with lacquer and vegetable dyes, so the toys are safe for babies to chew. The craft grew under **Tipu Sultan's** patronage, and later **Bavas Miyan** brought in Japanese techniques. Cheap plastic toys nearly killed it; revivals by state corporations and design firms brought it back, and Channapatna now sells to toy shops worldwide. Hold one and it feels like a pebble.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A traditional craft that fits the modern rule of non-toxic toys.
spotlights.memory_hook: Toy town, where the paint is safe to lick.

spotlights.name: Bidriware
spotlights.spot_it: Matt black metal vases, boxes and hookah bases inlaid with bright silver vines and flowers.
spotlights.story_md: **Bidriware** began in **Bidar** in the 14th century under the Bahmani sultans, with Persian influence. Artisans cast an alloy of **zinc and copper**, engrave patterns into it, hammer in silver wire or sheet, and then rub the piece with a paste of **soil from Bidar fort** mixed with ammonium chloride. The nitrate-rich soil turns the alloy jet black but leaves the silver shining. The craft received a GI tag in **2006**. Hyderabad and Lucknow also make it, but the soil, the name and the oldest workshops are Bidar's.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A medieval chemistry trick that is still a living trade.
spotlights.memory_hook: The fort's mud makes the metal black.

spotlights.name: Ilkal saree
spotlights.spot_it: A cotton saree with a broad red or maroon border and a red pallu crossed with white patterns, worn across north Karnataka.
spotlights.story_md: **Ilkal**, in Bagalkot district, has woven sarees for centuries; local tradition puts the start in the 8th century. About 20,000 people in the town are said to work in weaving. The body is cotton; border and pallu are art silk or silk. The signature is the **tope teni** join: the body and the pallu are linked on the loom by a loop technique, using three shuttles in the **kondi** method. A saree takes about seven days on a pit loom. Look for the red pallu with white patterns, and a border named for its motif, such as **gomi** or **chikki**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The everyday saree of north Karnataka and a living handloom economy.
spotlights.memory_hook: Red pallu, white patterns, looped join.

spotlights.name: Mysore Sandal Soap
spotlights.spot_it: A small oval bar in a cream box with a lion-bodied, elephant-headed beast on it, smelling of sandalwood.
spotlights.story_md: During the **First World War**, Mysore could not ship its huge stockpile of sandalwood to Europe. So in **1916** the Maharaja's government opened a soap factory in Bengaluru to use it, with Visvesvaraya among its backers. The soap, made with real sandalwood oil, became one of India's oldest continuous brands. Its logo is the **Sharabha**, a mythical beast with a lion's body and an elephant's head. The maker, **Karnataka Soaps and Detergents Ltd**, is still owned by the state, and the name is protected by a GI tag.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A wartime fix that became a 110-year-old brand.
spotlights.memory_hook: A war blocked the wood, so Mysore made soap.

sections.title: Dosa, coffee and the sweet named after a city
sections.intro_md:
Karnataka eats in at least four styles. **Old Mysore** cooking runs on rice, lentils and ragi, with mild, slightly sweet gravies. **Udupi** temple cooking is vegetarian, without onion or garlic, and spread across India through Udupi hotels. The **Mangalorean** coast cooks fish, coconut and fiery red chilli. **North Karnataka** eats jowar rotti, spicy brinjal and peanut chutney powder. And Kodagu has its pork curry.

Two inventions travelled furthest. The **masala dosa** in its classic form was popularised by Bengaluru and Udupi restaurants, and the **rava idli** was born in Bengaluru when rice ran short in the Second World War.

Behind both stands coffee. India's first coffee is said to have been planted in the hills of Chikkamagaluru in 1670, and Karnataka grows about seven of every ten cups India drinks.

spotlights.name: Masala dosa and the rava idli
spotlights.spot_it: A crisp golden crepe folded over spiced potato, with coconut chutney and sambar, in a Bengaluru darshini at 8 in the morning.
spotlights.story_md: Bengaluru's old restaurants built the dosa's reputation. **Mavalli Tiffin Room**, MTR, was opened in **1924** by the Maiya brothers from Udupi. During the Second World War, rice was scarce, so MTR's cooks made idlis from **semolina** instead: the **rava idli**. During the **Emergency** in 1975, price controls made serving food unprofitable, so MTR started packing spice mixes to keep staff employed; the brand was sold to Norway's Orkla in 2007 for US$80 million. Today the standing-room 'darshini' restaurant, serving dosa and coffee in minutes, is Bengaluru's signature.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A wartime shortage invented a breakfast all of India eats.
spotlights.memory_hook: No rice? Make the idli from rava.

spotlights.name: Bisi bele bath
spotlights.spot_it: A hot, soft mix of rice and toor dal cooked with tamarind, vegetables and a special spice powder, topped with ghee and crisp boondi.
spotlights.story_md: The name means 'hot lentil rice' in Kannada, and it must be eaten hot. Rice, toor dal and vegetables cook together with tamarind, jaggery and a roasted powder of chillies, coriander seeds, cinnamon, cloves, poppy seeds and dry coconut. It is finished with ghee, cashews and curry leaves and served with potato chips or boondi on top. Tradition links it to the kitchens of the Mysore palace. It is the dish most Kannadigas name first when asked what home tastes like.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The signature one-pot meal of Old Mysore.
spotlights.memory_hook: Hot, lentil, rice: the name is the instruction.

spotlights.name: Ragi mudde
spotlights.spot_it: Dense brown balls of finger millet on a plate, eaten by pinching off a piece and swallowing it with spicy saaru, not chewed.
spotlights.story_md: **Ragi**, finger millet, is the traditional staple of southern Karnataka's dry farmland. Ragi flour is stirred into boiling water until it forms a stiff dough, then shaped into balls. You break a piece, dip it in **saaru** or **soppu** curry made of greens, and swallow it whole. It is filling, high in calcium and fibre, and gives farm workers energy for hours. Long seen as poor people's food, it is now promoted in the state's school meals and in city restaurants as a 'millet' superfood.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A farm staple reborn as health food.
spotlights.memory_hook: Do not chew. Swallow the mudde.

spotlights.name: Mysore pak
spotlights.spot_it: Golden, porous squares of sweet that melt or crumble, made of gram flour, sugar and a great deal of ghee.
spotlights.story_md: Mysore pak was created in the palace kitchen of **Krishnaraja Wadiyar IV** in the early 20th century. Tradition says the cook **Kakasura Madappa** improvised with gram flour, ghee and sugar, and when the Maharaja asked the name, he called it after the city, plus **pak**, the sugar syrup it is cooked in. There are two styles today: the hard, porous, traditional one, and the soft, ghee-heavy version made famous by sweet shops in Bengaluru and Chennai. Madappa's descendants still run a sweet shop in Mysuru.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A royal kitchen invention that became south India's festival sweet.
spotlights.memory_hook: Named for the city by the cook, on the spot.

spotlights.name: Baba Budan and filter coffee
spotlights.spot_it: Frothy coffee poured back and forth between a steel tumbler and a wide steel bowl, the davara, to cool and foam it.
spotlights.story_md: The story goes that around **1670** a Sufi pilgrim, **Baba Budan**, returning from Mecca, smuggled **seven coffee beans** out of the Yemeni port of Mocha, perhaps in his beard, and planted them in the hills of Chikkamagaluru, now named **Baba Budangiri**. Whether or not every detail is true, those hills became India's first coffee country. Today Karnataka grows about **71 per cent** of India's coffee, mostly in Kodagu, Chikkamagaluru and Hassan, and more than 60 per cent of India's crop is robusta. At home it becomes **filter coffee**: dark decoction from a steel filter, boiled milk, sugar, and chicory.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Karnataka is India's coffee state.
spotlights.memory_hook: Seven smuggled beans, one coffee nation.

sections.title: Festivals
sections.intro_md:
Karnataka's festival year begins with **Ugadi**, the new year in March or April, when families eat **bevu-bella**, neem and jaggery mixed together, a reminder that the year will bring both bitter and sweet. **Sankranti** in January brings ellu-bella, sesame and jaggery, shared between neighbours. **Ganesha Chaturthi** and **Deepavali** are huge in the cities.

The state's own great festival is **Dasara** in Mysuru, held since 1610. On the coast, the winter season is **Kambala**, buffalo races through flooded paddy. In Bengaluru, the **Karaga** in spring and the **Kadalekai Parishe**, a groundnut fair, are survivals of the city's village past.

And on **1 November**, Kannada Rajyotsava, the red-and-yellow Kannada flag flies everywhere.

spotlights.name: Mysuru Dasara and the Jamboo Savari
spotlights.spot_it: A tusker carrying a golden howdah with the goddess Chamundeshwari, leading a procession through Mysuru, with a palace blazing with bulbs behind.
spotlights.story_md: Vijayanagara's kings held a great Mahanavami festival; the Wadiyars of Mysore continued it from **1610**, when Raja Wadiyar I began it at Srirangapatna. Dasara marks the goddess **Chamundeshwari** killing the buffalo-demon **Mahishasura**, from whom Mysuru takes its name. For ten nights the palace is lit with nearly **100,000 bulbs**. On Vijayadashami the **Jamboo Savari** sets off: a trained elephant carries the goddess in a golden howdah weighing about **750 kg**, followed by tableaux, bands and other elephants, to the Bannimantap, where a banni tree is worshipped. Elephants come in from forest camps weeks ahead to practise.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Karnataka's state festival, a royal ritual continued by a democracy.
spotlights.memory_hook: 750 kilograms of gold on one elephant's back.

spotlights.name: Kambala
spotlights.spot_it: Two buffaloes yoked together thundering through a flooded paddy track, a barefoot runner behind them, spray flying higher than their heads.
spotlights.story_md: **Kambala** is the buffalo race of Tulu Nadu, held from about November to March on tracks of slushy paddy field. Teams of two buffaloes are driven by a runner who holds the ropes and runs behind them. In some categories a wooden plank behind the animals throws up a sheet of water, and the height of the splash is judged. The Supreme Court banned it in **2014** on animal-welfare grounds; Karnataka passed an ordinance in **2017** and a law in 2018 to restore it. In 2020 a jockey, Srinivasa Gowda, was reported to have run 142.5 m in 13.62 s, and social media called him faster than Usain Bolt; the buffaloes, the water and the uncertified timing make that comparison meaningless.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A farming ritual turned mass sport, and a legal fight over animal welfare.
spotlights.memory_hook: The race where the buffaloes set the pace.

sections.title: How people live
sections.intro_md:
Community shapes politics and daily life. The two largest dominant groups are the **Lingayats**, strongest in the north, and the **Vokkaligas**, farmers of the south; most chief ministers have come from one or the other. A fresh social and economic survey in 2025 reopened old arguments about who counts as backward.

Daily rhythms are regional. A coastal family's day may end at a Yakshagana show; a Bengaluru engineer's is shaped by traffic and filter coffee; a north Karnataka farmer eats jowar rotti and watches the price of tur dal. Since the **Gokak agitation** of the 1980s, led by the actor Rajkumar, Kannada has been pushed into schools, offices and shop signs, and migrants to Bengaluru often feel the pressure.

spotlights.name: The Kodavas of Kodagu
spotlights.spot_it: Men in long black wrap-around coats with a sash and a silver dagger at the waist; women with the sari pleated at the back.
spotlights.story_md: The **Kodavas**, about 1.5 lakh people of Kodagu (Coorg), have customs found nowhere else in India. Men's formal dress is the **kupya**, a long dark coat with a red-and-gold sash holding the **peeche kathi** dagger. Women drape the sari with the pleats at the **back** and the end pinned at the right shoulder. Under India's Arms Act, Kodavas may carry guns without a licence, a colonial-era privilege. Their September festival **Kail Poldh** honours weapons. Kodagu gave India two army chiefs, Field Marshal **K. M. Cariappa** and General **K. S. Thimayya**, and hosts a hockey festival of clan teams.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A small community with an outsized role in India's army and hockey.
spotlights.memory_hook: Sari pleats at the back, gun without a licence.

sections.title: Bengaluru and how the state earns
sections.intro_md:
**Bengaluru** began in **1537** as a planned trading town. It became a British cantonment, then the capital of Mysore State, and after 1947 the home of public science and aerospace: the Indian Institute of Science, HAL, ISRO, Bharat Electronics. That pool of engineers is why software firms chose it from the 1980s. The old **Garden City** of Lalbagh and Cubbon Park is now India's biggest software exporter, famous also for traffic and for lakes choked with sewage foam.

The rest of the state earns from coffee, silk, sugarcane, iron ore, cement and tourism. In 2025-26 Karnataka's per capita income was about ₹3.86 lakh, against ₹2.05 lakh for India.

spotlights.name: Kempe Gowda and the four towers
spotlights.spot_it: A 108-foot bronze chieftain with a sword at the airport, and small stone watch towers in old Bengaluru.
spotlights.story_md: **Kempe Gowda I** (1510 to 1569), a chieftain under Vijayanagara, moved his seat from Yelahanka and built a fort and town in **1537**. He laid out streets by trade: Chickpete, Balepete for bangles, Tharagupete for grain. He dug lakes and tanks for water. He is also remembered for banning a cruel custom in which unmarried women's fingers were cut off in a ritual. Four towers marking the city's limits are traditionally credited to him or his successor; Lalbagh's tower on its ancient rock is one. A **108-foot statue** of him was unveiled at the airport that bears his name in 2022.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The planned trading town that grew into India's tech capital.
spotlights.memory_hook: A city born with its streets sorted by trade.

spotlights.name: Indian Institute of Science
spotlights.spot_it: Stone colonial buildings among huge trees in north Bengaluru, known locally as the Tata Institute.
spotlights.story_md: The idea came from **Jamsetji Tata**, who discussed it with **Swami Vivekananda** on a ship in 1893. The Maharaja of Mysore gave about **371 acres** of land, and the institute opened in **1909**. **C. V. Raman** became its first Indian director in 1933. IISc trained the scientists who later staffed HAL, ISRO and the defence labs, and that concentration of talent is the deep reason Bengaluru became India's technology city. It remains India's top-ranked research university.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The seed of Bengaluru's science and technology economy.
spotlights.memory_hook: A ship conversation in 1893 built a city's future.

spotlights.name: Infosys and Electronic City
spotlights.spot_it: Glass buildings, a pyramid and a dome on a manicured campus off the Hosur road: the Infosys headquarters in Electronic City.
spotlights.story_md: **Infosys** was founded on **2 July 1981** in Pune by seven engineers, including **N. R. Narayana Murthy** and **Nandan Nilekani**, with capital of about US$250, and moved to Bengaluru in 1983. In **1999** it became the first Indian company listed on the Nasdaq. By March 2026 it had about **3.29 lakh employees** and revenue of about ₹1.79 lakh crore. Its campus in **Electronic City**, the industrial park set up in the late 1970s, became the image of Indian IT. Sudha Murty, Narayana Murthy's wife, an engineer and writer, became one of India's best-loved authors.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The company that showed India could sell brains to the world.
spotlights.memory_hook: Seven founders, 250 dollars, three lakh jobs.

spotlights.name: Kolar Gold Fields
spotlights.spot_it: Old mine headframes and colonial bungalows in a dusty town east of Bengaluru, made famous again by the KGF films.
spotlights.story_md: At **Kolar Gold Fields**, the British firm John Taylor & Sons mined gold from 1880. In 1902 the mines were electrified by a 140-km line from Shivanasamudra. Nationalised in 1956, they produced over **900 tonnes** of gold before closing in **2001**, with gold still underground. The mines were among the deepest in the world, and that depth made them a physics lab: in **1965** an Indian-Japanese-British team detected **atmospheric neutrinos** at 2.3 km below ground here, the first time anyone had, publishing two weeks ahead of a South African team.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Gold paid for Mysore's modernity, and the empty mine gave physics a first.
spotlights.memory_hook: The first atmospheric neutrinos were caught in a gold mine.

sections.title: People to know
sections.intro_md:
You have met kings, saints, singers and writers. Here are three more Kannadigas whose stories travel: a leg spinner who later bowled with a broken jaw, a girl with no schooling who multiplied 13-digit numbers in her head, and a labourer who planted banyan trees because she had no children.

Other names worth knowing: **Rahul Dravid**, the Wall, from Bengaluru; **Prakash Padukone**, India's first All England badminton champion in 1980; **R. K. Narayan**, who set Malgudi in a town like his Mysuru; **Girish Karnad**, playwright and actor; **Field Marshal K. M. Cariappa** of Kodagu, the first Indian commander-in-chief; and **Sudha Murty**, engineer and author.

spotlights.name: Anil Kumble
spotlights.spot_it: A tall, bespectacled leg spinner with a fast, bouncing delivery, arms raised after a tenth wicket.
spotlights.story_md: **Anil Kumble**, born in Bengaluru in 1970, took **619 Test wickets** in 132 Tests, India's highest. In **February 1999**, in Delhi against Pakistan, he took all **10 wickets in an innings** for 74 runs, only the second man ever after England's Jim Laker in 1956. In 2002 in Antigua, a ball broke his jaw; he came back with his face strapped and bowled 14 overs, dismissing Brian Lara. He later captained and coached India. A Bengaluru road junction is named after him.
spotlights.why_it_matters: One of only three bowlers to take all ten wickets in a Test innings.
spotlights.memory_hook: Ten for 74, and later, one with a broken jaw.

spotlights.name: Shakuntala Devi
spotlights.spot_it: A smiling woman in a sari beside a blackboard of huge numbers, the 'human computer'.
spotlights.story_md: **Shakuntala Devi** (1929 to 2013) was born in Bengaluru, the daughter of a circus performer, and showed her gift for numbers as a small child without formal schooling. On **18 June 1980** at Imperial College London she multiplied two **13-digit numbers** chosen by a computer in **28 seconds**, a feat recorded by Guinness. She also wrote puzzle books and, in 1977, **The World of Homosexuals**, one of the first sympathetic Indian studies of the subject. A 2020 film starring Vidya Balan told her story.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A self-taught prodigy who also broke a social silence.
spotlights.memory_hook: Two 13-digit numbers, 28 seconds, no computer.

spotlights.name: Saalumarada Thimmakka
spotlights.spot_it: A tiny elderly woman in a green saree, beside a road lined with giant banyan trees.
spotlights.story_md: **Thimmakka**, a labourer from Gubbi in Tumakuru district, had no children. With her husband she began planting banyan saplings along the road between **Hulikal and Kudur**, carrying water to them in pots over kilometres. They planted about **385** trees along about 4.5 km, which now form a green tunnel, and hundreds more elsewhere. Saalu marada means 'row of trees'. She received the **Padma Shri** in 2019 and was named by the BBC among the world's 100 most influential women in 2016. She died in Bengaluru on **14 November 2025**, at a claimed age of 114.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Proof that one person can change a landscape.
spotlights.memory_hook: No children, so she raised 385 trees.

sections.title: Places to go
sections.intro_md:
A first trip can follow three loops. The **southern loop** runs from Bengaluru to Mysuru, Srirangapatna and Somanathapura, then up to Kodagu for coffee. The **heritage loop** goes north: Belur, Halebidu and Shravanabelagola, then Hampi, then Badami, Aihole and Pattadakal, and on to Vijayapura. The **coastal loop** runs from Mangaluru through Udupi, Murudeshwar and Gokarna, with Jog Falls and Agumbe as a detour.

Go between October and February for the heritage sites, and July to September for waterfalls and the green Ghats.

spotlights.name: Mysore Palace
spotlights.spot_it: A palace of grey granite with pink domes and a 44-metre tower, which on festival nights is outlined by nearly 100,000 bulbs.
spotlights.story_md: The old wooden palace of the Wadiyars burned down in **1897** during a wedding. The present palace, designed by the British architect **Henry Irwin** in an Indo-Saracenic mix of Hindu, Muslim, Rajput and Gothic styles, was finished in **1912**. Inside are a wedding hall with a stained-glass ceiling from Glasgow, a Durbar hall with a golden throne brought out only at Dasara, and painted walls showing the Dasara procession of the 1930s. It is one of the most visited monuments in India, with several million visitors a year.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The stage set of Karnataka's royal past and its biggest festival.
spotlights.memory_hook: Burned at a wedding, rebuilt as a wedding cake.

spotlights.name: Chikkamagaluru coffee hills
spotlights.spot_it: Rows of glossy coffee bushes under silver oaks on steep slopes, with Mullayanagiri's peak in cloud above.
spotlights.story_md: **Chikkamagaluru** district holds Karnataka's highest peak, **Mullayanagiri** at 1,925 metres, and the Baba Budangiri range where coffee first took root in India. Estates here grow arabica and robusta under a canopy of shade trees, often with pepper vines climbing the trunks, so one hill yields two crops. Homestays on estates let visitors walk through the plantations in the harvest season, December to February, when the red coffee cherries are picked by hand. The same hills give rise to the Tunga and Bhadra rivers.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Where Indian coffee began and still grows best.
spotlights.memory_hook: Coffee below, pepper climbing the trees above.

sections.title: What is happening now (2025 to 2026)
sections.intro_md:
The past eighteen months have been unusually eventful. In **May 2025** a Kannada book won the International Booker for the first time. In **June 2025**, celebrations of RCB's first IPL title turned into a deadly crowd crush outside Chinnaswamy Stadium. Bengaluru was reorganised under a new **Greater Bengaluru Authority**, and its metro grew to about 96 km. In **October 2025**, Kantara: Chapter 1 broke box-office records with a story of coastal spirit worship.

Politics turned too. In **March 2026** Siddaramaiah presented his last budget, built around the five 'guarantee' welfare schemes. In late **May 2026** he stepped down under a deal within the Congress party, and **D. K. Shivakumar** was sworn in as the 18th chief minister on **3 June 2026**, after a long, public power struggle.

spotlights.name: The Chinnaswamy crowd crush
spotlights.spot_it: Crowds climbing barricades and gates outside a cricket stadium in central Bengaluru, on the afternoon after a title win.
spotlights.story_md: On **4 June 2025**, a day after **Royal Challengers Bengaluru** won their first IPL title after 18 seasons, hundreds of thousands of fans gathered for celebrations at the **M. Chinnaswamy Stadium**. At about 3.30 p.m., crowds forced past barricades and climbed fences at several gates, and police used lathis. **Eleven people** died and 56 were injured. The state suspended five police officers including the city commissioner, the police filed a case against RCB, the event organiser and the state cricket association, and RCB's marketing head was arrested. It became a national debate about crowd safety.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A celebration that exposed how cities plan for crowds.
spotlights.memory_hook: The day after the cup, the crush.

spotlights.name: Greater Bengaluru Authority
spotlights.spot_it: A new map of Bengaluru split into five city corporations: Central, North, South, East and West.
spotlights.story_md: For decades one body, the **BBMP**, ran Bengaluru, and it had not had an elected council since 2020. On **15 May 2025** the state created the **Greater Bengaluru Authority** to replace it, with the power to set up to seven corporations under one umbrella. In 2025 it notified **five corporations** with **368 wards**, and the authority began full work on 2 September 2025. Supporters say smaller corporations can fix roads and drains faster; critics say the state government, which chairs the authority, keeps the real power. Elections to the new corporations were expected in 2026.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The biggest change to how India's tech capital is governed in decades.
spotlights.memory_hook: One city, five corporations, one boss.

spotlights.name: Kantara: Chapter 1
spotlights.spot_it: A film poster of a fierce figure with a painted face and a crown of palm fronds, over a forest at night.
spotlights.story_md: **Kantara: Chapter 1**, written, directed by and starring **Rishab Shetty**, was released on **2 October 2025**, the day of Vijayadashami. A prequel to the 2022 hit Kantara, it tells a mythic origin story for the **Panjurli** and **Guliga** daivas worshipped in Bhuta Kola on the Tulu coast. It grossed an estimated **₹850 crore** worldwide, became the second highest-grossing Kannada film ever and was reported as the highest-grossing Indian film of 2025. Its success took coastal ritual to a mass audience and reopened debates about whether sacred practices should be shown on screen.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Kannada cinema's biggest moment, built on a local ritual.
spotlights.memory_hook: A village spirit at the top of India's box office.

spotlights.name: A new chief minister
spotlights.spot_it: Two Congress leaders, one older and one younger, shaking hands at a press conference in Bengaluru.
spotlights.story_md: The Congress won the 2023 election with 135 of 224 seats, and **Siddaramaiah** became chief minister for a second time with **D. K. Shivakumar** as his deputy. For three years the two camps argued, in public, over a reported power-sharing deal. Siddaramaiah, who held the record for the longest combined tenure as chief minister, about eight years, presented the **2026-27 budget** on **6 March 2026**. At the end of May 2026 he resigned at the party's direction, and Shivakumar was sworn in as the **18th chief minister on 3 June 2026**. Shivakumar also kept the finance and Bengaluru development portfolios.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Karnataka's government changed hands without an election.
spotlights.memory_hook: Deputy for three years, chief minister on 3 June 2026.

sections.title: Recap
sections.intro_md:
**Where:** the south-west of the peninsula: coast, Ghats, plateau. Formed 1956, renamed 1973.

**History:** Ashoka at Maski; the Halmidi stone; Chalukya caves and Pattadakal; Hoysala soapstone; Gommateshwara; Vijayanagara until 1565; Gol Gumbaz; Tipu and his rockets; Kittur Chennamma.

**See it:** the stone chariot, Yakshagana crowns, Huli Vesha tigers, Mysore silk, Channapatna toys, Bidri, the Dasara elephant.

**Taste it:** masala dosa, rava idli, bisi bele bath, ragi mudde, Mysore pak, filter coffee.

**Now:** the first Kannada Booker, the Chinnaswamy crush, a new Bengaluru authority, Kantara, and a new chief minister since June 2026.

best_facts.fact: Around 1500, Vijayanagara, whose ruins are Hampi, is estimated to have been the second-largest city in the world after Beijing.
best_facts.why_surprising: A world metropolis that most people know only as ruins.

best_facts.fact: In 1965, physicists 2.3 km down in the Kolar Gold Fields made the first detection of atmospheric neutrinos, beating a South African team to publication by two weeks.
best_facts.why_surprising: A gold mine near Bengaluru scored a world first in particle physics.

best_facts.fact: Tipu Sultan's iron-cased rockets flew up to about 2 km; after 1799 Britain studied captured ones at Woolwich and William Congreve built his rockets from them.
best_facts.why_surprising: Western rocketry was copied from Mysore.

best_facts.fact: In the Gol Gumbaz, one handclap produced as many as 14 distinct echoes in experiments in 1945.
best_facts.why_surprising: A tomb that behaves like a sound machine.

best_facts.fact: The edict found at Maski in 1915 was the first to name Ashoka directly; before that he was known from inscriptions only as Devanampiya Piyadasi.
best_facts.why_surprising: A Karnataka boulder solved the identity of India's most famous emperor.

best_facts.fact: MTR's cooks invented the rava idli in Bengaluru during the Second World War because rice was scarce.
best_facts.why_surprising: A wartime shortage created a national breakfast.

best_facts.fact: Kannada writers have won eight Jnanpith awards, second only to Hindi's 12.
best_facts.why_surprising: A language of about one in twenty Indians has one in seven Jnanpiths.

best_facts.fact: Bidriware gets its jet-black colour from a paste made with soil from Bidar fort; the silver inlay stays bright.
best_facts.why_surprising: A fort's dirt is a craft ingredient.

best_facts.fact: Mysore Sandal Soap began in 1916 because the First World War stopped Mysore exporting its sandalwood to Europe.
best_facts.why_surprising: A war blockade created a 110-year-old brand.

best_facts.fact: Rajkumar, Kannada cinema's biggest star, was held for 108 days by the brigand Veerappan in 2000.
best_facts.why_surprising: A real kidnapping stranger than his films.

best_facts.fact: The golden howdah carried by the lead elephant in the Mysuru Dasara procession weighs about 750 kg.
best_facts.why_surprising: Three-quarters of a tonne of gold on one animal.

best_facts.fact: Kodavas are the only community in India allowed to carry guns without a licence, and their women pleat the sari at the back.
best_facts.why_surprising: Unique legal and dress customs in one small district.

best_facts.fact: Karnataka grows about 71 per cent of India's coffee, and tradition says it began with seven beans smuggled from Mocha by Baba Budan around 1670.
best_facts.why_surprising: A nation's coffee from a pilgrim's pocket.

best_facts.fact: Anil Kumble took all 10 Pakistan wickets in an innings in Delhi in 1999; only Jim Laker had done it before in Tests.
Shakuntala Devi, born in Bengaluru, multiplied two 13-digit numbers in her head in 28 seconds in 1980.
best_facts.why_surprising: Faster than many calculators of the time.

best_facts.fact: A Kambala jockey was reported to have run 142.5 m in 13.62 s in 2020, but the 'faster than Bolt' claim fails: buffaloes pulled him and the time was not certified.
best_facts.why_surprising: Viral maths that falls apart on inspection.

best_facts.fact: Gommateshwara at Shravanabelagola, carved around 983, is a 57-foot statue from a single granite block; it is next bathed in milk and saffron in 2030.
best_facts.why_surprising: A thousand-year-old monolith with a fixed 12-year bath schedule.

best_facts.fact: Banu Mushtaq's Heart Lamp, translated by Deepa Bhasthi, was the first Kannada book and the first short-story collection to win the International Booker, on 20 May 2025.
best_facts.why_surprising: Kannada fiction reached the top of world translation.

quiz_bank.explanation: Deepa Bhasthi, the first Indian translator to win the International Booker.

quiz_bank.prompt: What did Basava give every follower, regardless of caste?
quiz_bank.explanation: An ishtalinga, a personal linga worn on the body.

quiz_bank.prompt: At Udupi, the Kanakana Kindi window is linked to a saint who was kept out of the temple.
quiz_bank.explanation: Kanakadasa; Krishna is said to have turned to face him.

quiz_bank.prompt: In Yakshagana, who sings the story and directs the show?
quiz_bank.explanation: The bhagavata.

quiz_bank.prompt: Why is Purandara Dasa called the grandfather of Carnatic music?
quiz_bank.explanation: He created the graded teaching exercises in Mayamalavagowla still used today.
options: He systematised how it is taught
He founded the Mysore court orchestra
He wrote the first raga treatise

quiz_bank.prompt: What turns bidriware black?
quiz_bank.explanation: A paste with soil from Bidar fort and ammonium chloride.

quiz_bank.prompt: What is Channapatna's nickname?
quiz_bank.explanation: Gombegala Ooru, toy town.

quiz_bank.prompt: The rava idli was invented because rice was scarce in the Second World War.
quiz_bank.explanation: At MTR in Bengaluru, by its own account.

quiz_bank.prompt: Share of India's coffee grown in Karnataka: higher or lower than 50 per cent?
quiz_bank.explanation: About 71 per cent.

quiz_bank.prompt: About how much does the golden howdah in the Jamboo Savari weigh?
quiz_bank.explanation: About 750 kg.

quiz_bank.prompt: What happened to Kambala in 2014?
quiz_bank.explanation: The Supreme Court banned it; a 2017 ordinance and 2018 law restored it.

quiz_bank.prompt: Kodava women pleat the sari at the back.
quiz_bank.explanation: With the loose end pinned at the right shoulder.

quiz_bank.prompt: When is Kannada Rajyotsava?
quiz_bank.explanation: 1 November, the date the state was formed in 1956.

quiz_bank.prompt: Who founded Bengaluru, and when?
quiz_bank.explanation: Kempe Gowda I, in 1537.

quiz_bank.prompt: The first atmospheric neutrinos were detected in a gold mine in Karnataka.
quiz_bank.explanation: Kolar Gold Fields, 1965, at 2.3 km depth.

quiz_bank.prompt: Against which team did Anil Kumble take all 10 wickets in an innings?
quiz_bank.explanation: Pakistan, Delhi, February 1999: 10 for 74.

quiz_bank.prompt: What does 'Saalumarada' in Saalumarada Thimmakka mean?
quiz_bank.explanation: Row of trees: she planted about 385 banyans along a road.

quiz_bank.prompt: Why was the present Mysore Palace built?

side_dish.title: Why Agumbe drowns and Chitradurga thirsts
side_dish.body_md:
Drive 200 kilometres east from Agumbe and the rainfall drops from about 7,600 millimetres a year to well under 600. Same state, same monsoon. The difference is a mountain range.

From June, the south-west monsoon pushes warm, wet air off the Arabian Sea. When it hits the **Western Ghats**, a wall 1,000 to 1,900 metres high only 40 to 80 kilometres from the coast, the air has nowhere to go but up. As it rises it cools, roughly 6 to 10 °C for every 1,000 metres, and cool air cannot hold as much water vapour. The vapour condenses into cloud and falls as rain on the western slopes. This is called **orographic rain**, from the Greek for mountain.

By the time the air spills over the crest and sinks onto the Deccan, it has lost most of its moisture, and sinking air warms and dries further. The land behind the Ghats sits in a **rain shadow**. That is why Chitradurga, Ballari and Vijayapura are among the driest districts in south India, why the plateau is dotted with tanks built over centuries to catch every shower, and why the boulder hills of Hampi are bare.

It also explains the shape of the economy: coffee and spices in the wet Malnad, millets and sheep on the dry plateau, and every river that matters flowing east, carrying Ghats rain into the dry country.

offline_task.title: Make bisi bele bath
offline_task.body_md:
**Serves 3. About 45 minutes.**

**You need**
- 1/2 cup rice and 1/2 cup toor dal, washed
- 2 cups chopped mixed vegetables: carrot, beans, peas, potato, a few shallots
- A lemon-sized ball of tamarind soaked in 1/2 cup warm water, or 1 tbsp paste
- 1 tbsp jaggery, salt, 1/4 tsp turmeric
- 3 tbsp bisi bele bath powder (shop-bought MTR is fine), or make it: dry-roast 4 dry red chillies, 1 tbsp coriander seeds, 1 tsp chana dal, 1/2 tsp cumin, 1/2 tsp fenugreek, a small piece of cinnamon, 2 cloves and 2 tbsp dry coconut, then grind
- 3 tbsp ghee, a few cashews, curry leaves, mustard seeds, a pinch of hing
- Potato chips or boondi to serve

**Steps**
1. Pressure-cook the rice and dal together with 4 cups of water and the turmeric until very soft, about 4 whistles. Mash lightly.
2. In a pot, cook the vegetables in 1 cup of water with salt until just tender.
3. Add the tamarind water, jaggery and spice powder. Simmer 5 minutes.
4. Stir in the mashed rice and dal. Add hot water until it is loose, like a thick porridge. Simmer 5 more minutes.
5. Heat the ghee. Fry mustard seeds, hing, curry leaves and cashews. Pour over the pot.
6. Serve hot, with chips or boondi on top and a spoon of ghee.

**Notice**: it should be hot, tangy, a little sweet and soft enough to fall off the spoon. It thickens as it cools, so add water when reheating.
